cim: Nvidia stock falls after company opens probe into CEO Jensen Huang - ABC News
cim_eredeti: Nvidia stock falls after company opens probe into CEO Jensen Huang - ABC News
szoveg_eredeti:
Huang is no longer expected at a CEO forum hosted by Anthropic, sources said.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is no longer expected to attend a CEO forum hosted by artificial intelligence firm Anthropic on Monday, a source familiar told ABC News.

ElevenLabs, an AI audio research company, confirmed to ABC News that Huang dropped out of a separate event he was scheduled to speak at this week.

The developments came as Nvidia stock fell in the first trading session since the chip giant said it opened an investigation into Huang amid allegations of a Chinese intelligence-gathering effort targeting him.

Shares of Nvidia fell more than 5%, putting the stock price at $175.92.

The board of the California-based firm initiated an "independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company said in a statement Sunday.

The investigation will be overseen by a "committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel," Nvidia added.

Huang "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the Nvidia statement noted.

A group of top congressional and intelligence leaders known as the Gang of Eight is expected to receive a general national security briefing from CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Monday afternoon, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on CBS News Monday morning that the alleged Chinese intelligence-gathering effort involving Huang will likely "come up" during the briefing.

The Gang of Eight receives periodic intelligence briefings as part of Congress' oversight responsibilities. ABC News reached out to the CIA for comment on Monday's meeting.

While speaking to reporters on Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to discuss Nvidia’s investigation or national security implications related to the alleged Chinese intelligence-gathering effort.

"You have to ask the White House. I don't handle the that part of our operation,” he said.

Rubio also wouldn’t answer a question about Huang’s inclusion in the U.S. delegation for President Donald Trump's trip to China over the summer.

"I mean, I have a lot of jobs, but the White House Travel Office isn't one of them," he said.

Nvidia soared to prominence in recent years through selling many of the chips behind the AI boom. The company has defied skeptics with strong revenue quarter after quarter, despite political backlash against data centers and looming concern about a financial bubble in AI.

As of Monday morning, Nvidia boasted a value of more than $4 trillion as measured by market capitalization, making it the world's second-largest company. Apple is currently the largest.

Stocks in the U.S. climbed overall on Monday, recovering some of their losses from a selloff last Thursday.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average increased 2.1%, while the S&P 500 increased 2.3%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq jumped 2.5%.

The New York Times reported late last month that Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese espionage plot centered around a woman they identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials determined was funneling information to Beijing and had developed a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang.

The Chinese government denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."

Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after the New York Times story broke.

"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected" and are part of Jensen Huang's job, an Nvidia spokesperson told ABC News at the time.

However, Nvidia on Sunday shared with ABC News an internal message Jensen Huang sent to employees, in which he said he was "unfaithful" to his wife.

"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," the message said, in part. It did not name Alice Huang nor any other person.

Addressing Nvidia staff, partners and shareholders, Huang went on to say, "my responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang's message said.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

ABC News' Chris Watson, Lauren Peller, Allison Pecorin and John Parkinson contributed to this report.
